Graphical Quadratic Algebra
Dario Stein, Fabio Zanasi, Robin Piedeleu, Richard Samuelson

Abstract
Convex analysis and Gaussian probability are tightly connected, as mostly evident in the theory of linear regression. Our work introduces an algebraic perspective on such relationship, in the form of a diagrammatic calculus of string diagrams, called Graphical Quadratic Algebra (GQA). We show that GQA is a complete axiomatisation for the category of quadratic relations, a compositional formulation of quadratic problems. Moreover, we identify a sub-theory of GQA which is complete for the category of Gaussian probabilistic processes. We show how GQA may be used to study linear regression and probabilistic programming.



1
Introduction

Gaussian probability theory studies phenomena governed by
normal
distributions — bell-shaped curves fully determined by mean and variance. Quadratic optimisation, on the other hand, is concerned with minimising quadratic functions — those expressible as polynomials of degree at most 2. Though they arise in different contexts, these two areas are deeply related. A clear instance of this connection appears in linear regression, where one seeks the best-fitting solution to a linear system
Ax=b
, with
A
a matrix and
b
a vector representing observed data. If the error term
\epsilon
is assumed to follow a Gaussian distribution, then finding the most likely solution to the model
Ax+\epsilon=b
is equivalent to minimising the quadratic loss function
f(x)=||Ax-b||^{2}
, which measures the sum of squared residuals. The relationship goes further: the log-density of a Gaussian distribution is itself a quadratic function, and computing conditional distributions in Gaussian models often reduces to solving least-squares problems.

In this paper, we introduce a fresh perspective on Gaussian probability, quadratic optimisation, and their web of connections, by presenting them as categorical structures. Our main results are
complete axiomatisations
for these categories, via an axiomatic calculus called
graphical quadratic algebra
.

Our approach unfolds as follows. First, we study how quadratic problems
compose
, so that they can be organised into a category. To this aim, we view a partial quadratic function
F\colon\mathbb{R}^{m}\times\mathbb{R}^{n}\to[0,\infty]
as a
[0,\infty]
-weighted relation on
\mathbb{R}^{m}\times\mathbb{R}^{n}
, called
quadratic relation
. This perspective has three major appeals. First, quadratic relations characterise the solutions of constrained least-square problems (
[
9
]
). Second, their composition is naturally defined via constrained minimisation (see (
8
) below). Third, quadratic relations extend affine relations (
[
6
]
), linking our work with the theory of
Graphical Affine Algebra
(
[
6
]
) and offering a clear pathway towards a complete axiomatic calculus.

The resulting category
\mathbf{QuadRel}
, with morphisms the quadratic relations, provides an algebraic setting to study quadratic optimisation. Gaussian probability enters the picture as a subcategory
\mathbf{Gauss}
of
\mathbf{QuadRel}
. The category
\mathbf{Gauss}
has been previously studied as a
Markov category
, in the context of a more general framework for categorical probability theory
[
15
]
. Morphisms of
\mathbf{Gauss}
, called Gaussian stochastic maps, generalise Gaussian distributions in the same way as linear maps generalise vectors. The study of
\mathbf{Gauss}
is of independent interest because of its use as a semantics for Gaussian probabilistic programming (
[
30
]
).

Once the ‘semantic’ structures
\mathbf{QuadRel}
and
\mathbf{Gauss}
are in place, we introduce their ‘syntactic’ presentation. Our language adopts the graphical notation of
string diagrams
(see eg.
[
26
,
24
]
for recent introductions). As a two-dimensional formalism, string diagrams can be flexibly treated both as syntax and as combinatorial objects. They are now widely adopted in axiomatic reasoning on resource-sensitive models, eg. in linear algebra (
[
7
,
11
,
2
,
12
]
) and probabilistic reasoning (
[
15
,
18
,
22
,
19
]
), making it a natural choice for our approach.

The language we introduce, called
\mathbf{GQA}
(‘Graphical Quadratic Algebra’), consists of the string diagrams obtained by sequential and parallel composition of the following generators, for
k\in\mathbb{R}
:

(1)

\mathbf{GQA}
directly extends
Graphical Affine Algebra
(
\mathbf{GAA}
,
[
6
]
), which is given by the generators of the first two blocks in (
1
). Semantically, the generators in the first block model basic linear algebraic operations of copying (
), discarding (
) addition (
), scaling (
\scriptstyle k
), and the constants zero (
) and one (
). With the equational theory of Hopf bimonoids (Fig.
1
, first block), string diagrams built with these generators are known to axiomatise the category
\mathbf{AffVect}
of affine maps (
[
6
]
). If we add the generators of the second block of (
1
), namely

\lxSVG@closescope {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}
, with behaviour symmetric to their mirrored version and extra equations (third block in Fig.
1
, notably including two Frobenius monoid structures), we obtain the full
\mathbf{GAA}
, which axiomatises the category
\mathbf{AffRel}
of affine relations, i.e. affine subspaces that compose relationally (
[
6
]
).

The surprising discovery of our work is that, in order to extend the axiomatisation of the category
\mathbf{AffRel}
of affine relations to one of the category
\mathbf{QuadRel}
of
quadratic
relations, it suffices to add just one extra generator,
(and three equations as in Fig.
1
, second block): this yields
\mathbf{GQA}
. Moreover, we axiomatise
\mathbf{Gauss}
by restricting
\mathbf{GQA}
to generators in the first and third block in (
1
).

Axioms of Graphical Quadratic Algebra

In
\mathbf{Gauss}
,
is interpreted as the standard normal distribution
\mathcal{N}(0,1)
, and in
\mathbf{QuadRel}
as the quadratic function
f(x)=\frac{1}{2}x^{2}
(ie., a unary quadratic relation on
\mathbb{R}
). We illustrate this dual interpretation via an example.

(2)

In
\mathbf{Gauss}
, (
2
) means that if
X_{1},X_{2}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)
are independent variables, then
Y=X_{1}+X_{2}
has distribution
\mathcal{N}(0,2)
.

We can now use the axioms of GQA (Fig.
1
) to derive (
2
). The notable step involves the axiom scheme
RI
, expressing that the function
f(x,y)=\frac{1}{2}(x^{2}+y^{2})
is
invariant under rotations
. When interpreted in
\mathbf{Gauss}
,
RI
is evocative of the Herschel-Maxwell theorem, which states that the normal distribution is uniquely characterised by its rotation invariance (e.g.
[
16
]
).
Because
\cos(\pi/4)=\sin(\pi/2-\pi/4)=\sin(\pi/4)=1/\sqrt{2}
, we can apply
RI
with
\varphi=\pi/4
as below. We then simplify the resulting string diagram via linear algebraic manipulations in the fragment GAA, obtaining the desired outcome
\sqrt{2}
.

\mathrel{\overset{\makebox[0.0pt]{\mbox{\tiny RI}}}{=}}
\sqrt{2}
\scriptstyle cos(\pi/4)
\scriptstyle-sin(\pi/4)
\scriptstyle sin(\pi/4)
\scriptstyle cos(\pi/4)
\mathrel{\overset{\makebox[0.0pt]{\mbox{\tiny GAA}}}{=}}
-1
\sqrt{2}
\mathrel{\overset{\makebox[0.0pt]{\mbox{\tiny Z}}}{=}}
\sqrt{2}
\mathrel{\overset{\makebox[0.0pt]{\mbox{\tiny GAA}}}{=}}

Completeness of
\mathbf{GQA}
for
\mathbf{QuadRel}
and
\mathbf{Gauss}
ensures that any semantic equality as in Example
1
can in principle be derived. More broadly, this algebraic characterisation sheds light on the connections between quadratic optimisation and Gaussian probability theory, revealing their relative expressive power. Notably, the equational theory of
\mathbf{Gauss}
is a fragment of the one of
\mathbf{QuadRel}
, without the ability to model relational behaviours using Frobenius monoids. Moreover, the presentation of
\mathbf{Gauss}
omits the generator
, which we may regard as conditioning of Gaussians. From this perspective, we may view quadratic relations as generalised Gaussian distributions, which combine probability and conditioning.

There are a few more interesting ramifications of our work. As noted, there are transformations relating Gaussian distributions, quadratic problems, and affine spaces. However, turning them into functors is technically challenging, as studied in
[
29
]
. Thanks to our axiomatic presentations, it suffices to define these mappings on the generators of
\mathbf{GQA}
to obtain functoriality as a simple corollary. We explore this in
Section

5.1
.

Our characterisations also enable a new methodology, based on equational diagrammatic reasoning, to study domains modelled by quadratic relations or Gaussian distributions, such as linear regression and probabilistic program semantics. We explore these examples in Section
5
. As a preview, the program below left is written in a language with support for Gaussian distributions and a conditioning operator
(=:=)
, and computes inference of a latent variable from a noisy observation. The corresponding
\mathbf{GQA}
-diagram is below right.

\displaystyle\mathrm{let}\,{\text{value}}\,={50+10\cdot\mathrm{normal}()}\,\mathrm{in}\,

\displaystyle\mathrm{let}\,{\text{measurement}}\,={\text{value}+5\cdot\mathrm{normal}()}\,\mathrm{in}\,

\displaystyle\text{measurement}\mathrel{\scalebox{0.4}[1]{${=}$}{:}{\scalebox{0.4}[1]{${=}$}}}\underline{40};

value

10
5
conditioning
adding noise
prior
40
50

Programs in this language correspond systematically to string diagrams. Moreover, the axioms of
\mathbf{GQA}
suffice to reduce such a diagram to one representing the posterior distribution, effectively mirroring the program’s execution.

Synopsis
After preliminaries (
Section

2
), we present our work in two steps: first we introduce the simpler theory
\mathbf{Gauss}
, and show how the fragment
\overrightarrow{\mathbf{GQA}}
axiomatises it (
Section

3
). Next, we introduce
\mathbf{QuadRel}
and its axiomatic calculus, the full
\mathbf{GQA}
(
Section

4
). We then conclude with some applications (
Section

5
) and future work (
Section

6
). Missing proofs and details are in appendices.

2
Background: Graphical Affine Algebra

We recall background on string diagrams and Graphical Affine Algebra, referring to
[
6
]
for more details. A symmetric strict monoidal category with set of objects the natural numbers, and monoidal product on objects given by addition, is called a
prop
(
[
23
]
). Prop morphisms are identity-on-objects symmetric monoidal functors between props. Props play a role akin to algebraic clones, in a monoidal setting. Various linear algebraic transformations may be organised into props.

Definition 1

The prop
\mathbf{AffVect}
has affine maps of type
\mathbb{R}^{m}\to\mathbb{R}^{n}
as morphisms
m\to n
, with composition given by matrix multiplication and monoidal product given by direct sum.
The prop
\mathbf{AffRel}
has affine subspaces of
\mathbb{R}^{m+n}
as morphisms
m\to n
, with relational composition
R;S=\{(\mathbf{v},\mathbf{w})\mid\exists\mathbf{u}.(\mathbf{v},\mathbf{u})\in R\wedge(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{w})\in S\}
, and monoidal product given by direct sum.

Because of the way they compose,
\mathbf{AffRel}
-morphisms are called
affine relations
. Complete axiomatisations for these categories are provided by string diagrammatic calculi, which we now introduce. A
symmetric monoidal theory
(SMT) is a pair
(\Sigma,E)
, where
\Sigma
is a signature of operations
o\colon m\to n
with an arity
m
and coarity
n
, and
E
is a set of equations between
\Sigma
-terms. A
\Sigma
-term
c
of type
m\to n
will be represented graphically as
a string diagram
(
[
24
,
26
]
) with
m
dangling wires on the left and
n
on the right, also written
c
m
n
. Formally,
\Sigma
-terms are freely obtained by sequential and parallel compositions of the operations in
\Sigma
together with the identity

Given an SMT
(\Sigma,E)
, the prop
\mathsf{FreeP}_{\scriptscriptstyle(\Sigma,E)}
freely generated by
(\Sigma,E)
has morphisms
m\to n
the string diagrams of type
m\to n
quotiented by
E
, with sequential and parallel composition defined as on the corresponding
\Sigma
-terms. We will typically regard
\mathsf{FreeP}_{\scriptscriptstyle(\Sigma,E)}
as a
string diagrammatic calculus
, with the string diagrams being its (graphical)
syntax
. The props defined ‘directly’, as
\mathbf{AffVect}
and
\mathbf{AffRel}
, are regarded as
semantic models
for diagrammatic calculi. When there is an isomorphism of props
\left\llbracket{\cdot}\right\rrbracket
between
\mathsf{FreeP}_{\scriptscriptstyle(\Sigma,E)}
and another prop
\mathbf{C}
, we say that
\mathbf{C}
is
presented
(or axiomatised) by
(\Sigma,E)
. Because prop morphisms are identity-on-objects, to prove such result it suffices to prove that
\left\llbracket{\cdot}\right\rrbracket
is full and faithful. In logical terms, we can phrase these requirements as
soundness
(if
s=t
in
\mathsf{FreeP}_{\scriptscriptstyle(\Sigma,E)}
, then
\left\llbracket{s}\right\rrbracket=\left\llbracket{t}\right\rrbracket
),
completeness
(if
\left\llbracket{s}\right\rrbracket=\left\llbracket{t}\right\rrbracket
in
\mathbf{C}
, then
s=t
in
\mathsf{FreeP}_{\scriptscriptstyle(\Sigma,E)}
) and
definability
(for every
f\colon m\to n
in
\mathbf{C}
, there exists a
\Sigma
-term
s:m\to n
with
\left\llbracket{s}\right\rrbracket=f
).

)

Importantly, Proposition
1
implies that, whenever we reason in the aforementioned calculi, any equivalence of matrices or subspaces represented by string diagrams are provable in the corresponding equational theory. This will allow us to use freely known facts of linear algebra (e.g. those recalled in Appendix
B
) in diagrammatic reasoning whenever needed, allowing us to focus on the quadratic extension that is the topic of this paper.

(5)

Here ,
\underline{A}
represents
A
in the sense that it is interpreted as
A\colon n\to m
via the isomorphism
\overrightarrow{\mathbf{GAA}}\to\mathbf{AffVect}
, and as
\{(\mathbf{v},\mathbf{w})\mid\mathbf{w}=A\mathbf{v}\}
via the isomorphism
\mathbf{GAA}\to\mathbf{AffRel}
. Similarly, a subspace
S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{m+n}
may be represented by the string diagram
\underline{A}
in
\mathbf{GAA}
, for any
A
such that
\mathrm{im}(A)=S
. We will also write this as
\underline{S}
. Well-definedness of this encoding is justified by
Proposition

8
, App.
B
. Finally, given a scalar
c\in\mathbb{R}
, we sometimes abbreviate
c
with
\underline{c}
.

3
Axiomatising Gaussian Probability

3.1
Gaussian Probability

Gaussian probability is an expressive self-contained fragment of probability theory. We recall what is strictly necessary here, referring to e.g.
[
3
]
for further background. A random variable
X
is called
normally distributed
or
Gaussian
with mean
\mu\in\mathbb{R}^{n}
and variance
\sigma^{2}
for
\sigma\in[0,\infty)
, if it has density function

f(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^{2}}}\exp\left(-\frac{(x-\mu)^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}}\right)

with respect to the Lebesgue measure. This is typically written
X\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^{2})
, meaning the distribution
\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^{2})
, also called Gaussian distribution, is the law of
X
. The
standard normal distribution

\mathcal{N}(0,1)
is particularly significant, as it generates any other normal distribution, in the following sense:
a random vector
\mathbf{X}
is
multivariate normal
if its distribution arises as
\mathbf{X}=A\cdot(Z_{1},\ldots,Z_{k})+\mathbf{\mu}
,
where
Z_{1},\ldots,Z_{k}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)
are independent variables and
A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times k}
is a matrix and
\mathbf{\mu}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}
. In other words, multivariable normal distributions arise as the pushforwards of standard normal distributions under affine maps. The distribution of
\mathbf{X}
is fully characterised by its mean
\mathbf{\mu}
and its covariance matrix
\Sigma=AA^{T}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}
, for
A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times k}
. Conversely, every positive semidefinite matrix
\Sigma
is the covariance matrix of a unique Gaussian distribution
\mathcal{N}(\mu,\Sigma)
, supported on the affine subspace
\mu+\mathrm{im}(\Sigma)
.
A convenient way of building up complicated Gaussian distributions is by pushing forward existing distributions under affine maps: if
\mathcal{N}(\mu,\Sigma)
is a Gaussian distribution and
A
is a matrix, then the pushforward distribution
A_{*}\mathcal{N}(\mu,\Sigma)
is
\mathcal{N}(A\mu,A\Sigma A^{T})
. If we aim to include Gaussian distributions and affine maps in the same categorical structure, it is natural to study
Gaussian maps
, which are a simple kind of stochastic map consisting of an affine function with Gaussian noise, informally written
f(x)=Ax+\mathcal{N}(b,\Sigma)
, with
A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times m}
,
b\in\mathbb{R}^{n}
and
\Sigma\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}
.
To compose this with another Gaussian map
g(y)=Cy+\mathcal{N}(d,\Xi)
, we combine their Gaussian noise independently using the transformation rule
g(f(x))=CAx+\mathcal{N}(Cb+d,C\Sigma C^{T}+\Xi)
.

Definition 2
(
[
15
, § 6]
)

The prop
\mathbf{Gauss}
has as morphisms
m\to n
the tuples
(A,b,\Sigma)
with
A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times m}
,
b\in\mathbb{R}^{n}
and positive semidefinite
\Sigma\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}
. Composition and monoidal product are given by

\displaystyle(A,b,\Sigma);(C,d,\Xi)

\displaystyle=(CA,Cb+d,C\Sigma C^{T}+\Xi)

\displaystyle(A_{1},b_{1},\Sigma_{1})\oplus(A_{2},b_{2},\Sigma_{2})

\displaystyle=\begin{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}\scriptstyle A_{1}\!\!&\!\!\scriptstyle 0\\
\scriptstyle 0&\scriptstyle A_{2}\end{pmatrix},\begin{pmatrix}\scriptstyle b_{1}\\
\scriptstyle b_{2}\end{pmatrix},\begin{pmatrix}\scriptstyle\Sigma_{1}\!\!&\!\!\scriptstyle\scriptstyle 0\\
\scriptstyle 0\!&\!\scriptstyle\Sigma_{2}\end{pmatrix}\end{pmatrix}

Gaussian distributions are the ‘states’
0\to n
in
\mathbf{Gauss}
. There is a prop morphism
\mathbf{Vect}\to\mathbf{Gauss}
representing an affine map
x\mapsto Ax+b
as the Gaussian map
(A,b,0)
.

, the term ‘causal’ indicates that the operations in (

) should be read as processing values from left-to-right, without constraining the values of inputs. Note we may regard
\overrightarrow{\mathbf{GQA}}
as an extension of
\overrightarrow{\mathbf{GAA}}
from Section

. The extension is simply given by adding the operation
and the associated equations. It is also a fragment of full
\mathbf{GQA}
, which we will introduce later.

\left\langle{\cdot}\right\rangle
of
\overrightarrow{\mathbf{GQA}}
-generators as morphisms of
\mathbf{Gauss}
. We use the notation
f(x)=Ax+\mathcal{N}(b,\Sigma)
for such a morphism of type
m\to n
.

4
Axiomatising Quadratic Problems

As mentioned in the introduction, Gaussian probability and quadratic problems are tightly related. We will now introduce
quadratic relations
as a categorical formalism to express quadratic problems in a compositional way. We then give a presentation
\mathbf{GQA}
for this category, and use this presentation to study the relationship with Gaussian probability in an algebraic fashion.

4.1
Quadratic Problems as Quadratic Relations

We justify the introduction of quadratic relations in steps. The basic setup of an optimisation problem is: given a weight (or cost) function
f(x_{1},\ldots,\allowbreak x_{m+n})
, compute the parameterised infimum
(x_{1},\ldots,\allowbreak x_{m})\mapsto\inf\{f(x_{1},\ldots,\allowbreak x_{m+n}):

(x_{m+1},\dots,\allowbreak x_{m+n})\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\}
over some variables. We can type such a weight function as
F:\mathbb{R}^{m}\times\mathbb{R}^{n}\to[0,+\infty]
, thereby formally specifying the ‘input’ and ‘output’ variables. How to compose such functions? We can see
F:\mathbb{R}^{m}\times\mathbb{R}^{n}\to[0,+\infty]
as a
weighted relation
the same way that an ordinary relation can be seen as
R:\mathbb{R}^{m}\times\mathbb{R}^{n}\to\{0,1\}
. This suggests a notion of composition: while relations compose as on the left below,
weighted relations compose by adding the weights and minimising over the shared variable
3
3

3

This analogy can be made rigorous with quantales (
[
21
]
). Our weighted relations are parametrised over the quantale
([0,+\infty],\geq,+)
.
, as on the right below:

(R;S)(x,z)=\bigvee_{y}R(x,y)\cdot S(y,z)\qquad(F;G)(x,z)=\inf_{{y}}\left\{{F(x,y)+G(y,z)}\right\}

(8)

This way of building up optimisation problems is well-established, see e.g.
[
17
]
for model-predictive control,
[
25
]
for convex analysis (where weighted relations are called
bifunctions
),
[
33
]
for control theory, and
[
29
]
for a categorical perspective. In our developments, it is convenient to introduce the following notation, reminiscent of Iverson brackets (
[
25
]
), associating a weighted relation
\{\!|\,{\phi}\,|\!\}
to a formula
\phi
, denoting a linear equation between its free variables:

\{\!|\,{\phi}\,|\!\}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathrm{def.}}}{{=}}0\quad\text{if $\phi$ is true},\quad\infty\quad\text{otherwise}

(9)

Note that
0
denotes truth and
\infty
falsity in this context! The indicator function of a set
A
is given by
1_{A}(x)=\{\!|\,{x\in A}\,|\!\}
.

Example 2

Consider the weighted relation
F:\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^{2}\to[0,\infty]
given by the constraint

F(c,(x,y))=\{\!|\,{c=x+y}\,|\!\}
, and let
G:\mathbb{R}^{2}\times\mathbb{R}^{0}\to[0,\infty]
be
G((x,y),())=\frac{1}{2}(x^{2}+y^{2})
. Then the composite
F;G
computes the parameterised quadratic problem
(F;G)(c,())=\inf\left\{{\frac{1}{2}(x^{2}+y^{2}):x+y=c}\right\}=\frac{1}{4}c^{2}
. We will render this composition diagrammatically in
\mathbf{GQA}
,
cf.

Example

4
.

We now focus on the class of weighted relations, called
quadratic relations
, which correspond to quadratic problems: this is a type of optimisation problem involving quadratic objective functions and affine constraints. First, a
quadratic function

f:\mathbb{R}^{n}\to\mathbb{R}
is a function that can be written as a multivariate polynomial of degree at most
2
. Examples of quadratic functions are the squared euclidean distance
||\mathbf{x}||^{2}
,
(x_{1}-1)x_{2}
, and
x_{1}^{2}-x_{2}
. A
partial quadratic function
is allowed to assume the value
+\infty
(indicating falsity/partiality) outside an affine subspace
M
.

Definition 3
(
[
25
, p.109]
)

A
partial quadratic function

f:\mathbb{R}^{n}\to[-\infty,\infty]
is a function that can be written in form

f(x)=\langle x,\Sigma x\rangle+\langle b,x\rangle+c+\{\!|\,{x\in M}\,|\!\}

where
M\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n}
is an affine subspace,
\Sigma\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}
is a symmetric matrix,
b\in\mathbb{R}^{n}
,
c\in\mathbb{R}
, and
\langle-,-\rangle
denotes the standard inner product on
\mathbb{R}^{n}
.

Recall that a function
f:\mathbb{R}^{n}\to[-\infty,\infty]
is
convex
if its epigraph
\{(x,y):y\geq f(x)\}
is a convex subset of
\mathbb{R}^{n+1}
. An
elementary convex partial quadratic function
is one in diagonal form
h(x)=\sum_{i}\lambda_{i}x_{i}^{2}
with
\lambda_{i}\in[0,+\infty]
. The function
h
is partial, because
h(x)=\infty
whenever
\lambda_{i}=\infty
and
x_{i}\neq 0
.

Example 3

The negative log-density function of a Gaussian distribution on
\mathbb{R}^{n}
is a partial convex quadratic function on
\mathbb{R}^{n}
. It is partial because it takes the value
+\infty
(corresponding to density
0
) outside of its support subspace
S
.

It turns out that nonnegative partial quadratic functions are automatically convex. Also, they are closed under the composition formula (
8
). We state a slightly more general proposition, namely closure under arbitrary constrained infima (see Appendix
E
).

Proposition 2

If
M\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n}\times\mathbb{R}^{m}
is an affine subspace, and
g
is a nonnegative partial quadratic function, then so is
f(x)=\inf\left\{{g(y)\mid(x,y)\in M}\right\}
.

Definition 4
(Quadratic Relations)

The prop
\mathbf{QuadRel}
of quadratic relations has:

•

morphisms
m\to n
are non-negative partial quadratic functions
F:\mathbb{R}^{m}\times R^{n}\to[0,\infty]
, called
quadratic relations

•

identities are indicator functions
\mathsf{id}_{n}(x,y)=\{\!|\,{x=y}\,|\!\}

•

composition is by minimisation: for
F\colon m\to n
and
G\colon n\to p
, define
F;G:m\to p
as
(F;G)(x,z):=\inf_{{y}}\left\{{F(x,y)+G(y,z)}\right\}
.

•

the monoidal product is addition. Given
F_{i}\colon{m_{i}}\to{n_{i}}
for
i=1,2
, then
F_{1}\oplus F_{2}\colon{m_{1}+m_{2}}\to{n_{1}+n_{2}}
is defined by

(F_{1}\oplus F_{2})((x_{1},x_{2}),(y_{1},y_{2}))=F_{1}(x_{1},y_{1})+F_{2}(x_{2},y_{2}).

Composition in
\mathbf{QuadRel}
is well-defined by
Proposition

2
, since we can write
(F;G)(x,z)=

\text{inf}\{H(\mathbf{y}):

(x,z,\mathbf{y})\in M\}
where
H(y_{1},y_{2},y_{3},y_{4})=F(y_{1},y_{2})+G(y_{3},y_{4})
and
M=\{(x,z,y_{1},y_{2},y_{3},y_{3}):x=y_{1},y_{2}=y_{3},z=y_{4}\}
.
To every affine relation
M\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{m}\times\mathbb{R}^{n}
, we can associate the quadratic relation
1_{M}
given by its indicator function. This assignment respects composition, i.e. yields a prop morphism
\mathbf{AffRel}\to\mathbf{QuadRel}
.

is freely generated by the following operations and the equations in Figure

, for
k\in\mathbb{R}

from Section

and

We now define an interpretation of
\overrightarrow{\mathbf{GQA}}
-generators as morphisms of
\mathbf{QuadRel}
. To each operation
c
of type
m\to n
we assign a quadratic relation
\left\llbracket{c}\right\rrbracket
of the same type, i.e. a nonnegative partial quadratic function
\mathbb{R}^{m+n}\to[0,\infty]
. We make use of the notation
\{\!|\,{\phi}\,|\!\}
introduced in (
9
).

4.3
Completeness of
\mathbf{GQA}
for
\mathbf{QuadRel}

In this section we establish that
\mathbf{GQA}
presents
\mathbf{QuadRel}
. For this, we need to prove soundness, completeness and definability.
Soundness is a routine check on the axioms (Proposition
11
). We focus on definability and completeness.

First, in a category where objects are equipped with Frobenius monoids, questions about arbitrary morphisms can be reduced to questions about states, i.e. morphisms
0\to n
, as follows: for a morphism
f:m\to n
, its ‘name’
\lceil f\rceil:0\to m\oplus n
is defined as

\lceil f\rceil
=
f

(10)

The assignment
f\mapsto\lceil f\rceil
is bijective – every morphism can be recovered from its name by bending back the top wire, composing with
and using axiom
\bullet
-
fr
and
coun
.

It will be useful to introduce a subprop
\overrightarrow{\mathbf{GQA}}_{\scriptscriptstyle{E}}
of
\mathbf{GQA}
, defined as follows.

Definition 5

The prop
\overrightarrow{\mathbf{GQA}}_{\scriptscriptstyle{E}}
is freely generated as
\overrightarrow{\mathbf{GQA}}
with the addition of the generator
and equations, for
k\in\mathbb{R}\!\setminus\!\{0\}

Diagrams in
\overrightarrow{\mathbf{GQA}}_{\scriptscriptstyle{E}}
are not only a useful intermediary step in the proof of completeness; it turns out they axiomatise the
extended Gaussians
of
[
28
,
29
]
, which can be thought of intuitively as Gaussian maps that incorporate a form of (non-probabilistic) nondeterminism, modelled by the extra generator
(see Appendix
F
for details). In this paper, we focus on
\mathbf{GQA}
, and leave further exploration of
\overrightarrow{\mathbf{GQA}}_{\scriptscriptstyle{E}}
to future work.

A fundamental piece of the completeness proof involves showing that any quadratic problem, represented as a string diagram of
\mathbf{GQA}
with no inputs, can be turned into a string diagram of the fragment
\overrightarrow{\mathbf{GQA}}_{\scriptscriptstyle{E}}
. This crucial step is Theorem
4.1
below, an elimination procedure which, given a state in
\mathbf{GQA}
, iteratively removes all occurrences of conditioning on some variable being zero (
).
The elimination procedure can therefore be understood as symbolically conditioning an (extended)
Gaussian to obtain an explicit posterior, or as solving a quadratic problem via QR decomposition.

Theorem 4.1

Let
M:0\to n
be a string diagram in
\mathbf{GQA}
. Then there exists a string diagram
M^{\prime}
in
\overrightarrow{\mathbf{GQA}}_{\scriptscriptstyle{E}}
, and a ‘scalar’
\alpha:0\to 0
, such that
M=M^{\prime}\oplus\alpha
is derivable in
\mathbf{GQA}
. The scalar is of the form
\underline{c}
with
c\in[0,\infty)
, or
.

Theorem 4.2

The prop
\mathbf{QuadRel}
is presented by
\mathbf{GQA}
.

For completeness, it suffices to show that for all states
M_{1},M_{2}\colon 0\to n
of
\mathbf{GQA}
, if
\left\llbracket{M_{1}}\right\rrbracket=\left\llbracket{M_{2}}\right\rrbracket
in
\mathbf{QuadRel}
, then
M_{1}=M_{2}
is derivable in
\mathbf{GQA}
. The steps of the proof are as follows (see Appendix
G
for details). First, using
Theorem

4.1
, we transform each
M_{i}
(for
i=1,2
) into the form
M_{i}^{\prime}
\underline{c_{i}}
, where
M_{i}^{\prime}
lies in
\overrightarrow{\mathbf{GQA}}_{\scriptscriptstyle{E}}
. Then, to each
M_{i}^{\prime}
, we apply the normalisation procedure for states in
\overrightarrow{\mathbf{GQA}}_{\scriptscriptstyle{E}}
(
Proposition

17
), which brings them to the form

, where
D_{i}
is a vector subspace,
\mu_{i}\in{D_{i}}^{\bot}
,
L_{i}
is lower triangular, and
\mathrm{im}(L_{i}{L_{i}}^{T})\subseteq{D_{i}}^{\bot}
. By
Proposition

26
),
\left\llbracket{N_{1}}\right\rrbracket=\left\llbracket{N_{2}}\right\rrbracket
if and only if
D_{1}=D_{2}
,
\mu_{1}=\mu_{2}
, and
L_{1}L_{1}^{T}=L_{2}L_{2}^{T}
. Using
Proposition

14
, we can assume that
L_{1}=L_{2}
in the two diagrams. Then, by appealing to the completeness of
\mathbf{GAA}
, we can show that
N_{1}=N_{2}
. Finally, since
M_{i}=N_{i}
, we can conclude
M_{1}=M_{2}
, as we wanted.

5
Applications

5.1
Functorial Transformations

A powerful application of our presentations for
\mathbf{Gauss}
and
\mathbf{QuadRel}
is the ease with which we can now define functors on these categories, as mappings on generators preserving the relevant equations. By the universal property of a presentation, such an assignment extends uniquely to a morphism of props. The first functor we consider clarifies the connection between Gaussian probability and quadratic problems. Relying on the isomorphisms
\mathbf{Gauss}\cong\overrightarrow{\mathbf{GQA}}
and
\mathbf{QuadRel}\cong\mathbf{GQA}
, we can define a functor
L:\mathbf{Gauss}\to\mathbf{QuadRel}
simply by mapping the generators of
\overrightarrow{\mathbf{GQA}}
to the same generators in
\mathbf{GQA}
. Note that
L
is functorial by construction, even though composition operations in
\mathbf{Gauss}
(integration/pushforward) and composition in
\mathbf{QuadRel}
(infimisation) are at first glance very different. It remains to compute how the functor
L
acts concretely on a Gaussian map (see Appendix
H
for details).

Proposition 3

The functor
L
sends a Gaussian map
f(x)=Ax+\mathcal{N}(\mu,\Sigma)
to the quadratic relation given by its negative conditional log-density. That is,

Lf(x,y)
is defined as
\frac{1}{2}\langle(y-Ax-\mu),\Omega(y-Ax-\mu)\rangle+\{\!|\,{(y-Ax-\mu)\in\mathrm{im}(\Sigma)}\,|\!\}
,
where
\Omega
is a generalised inverse of
\Sigma
, i.e. satisfies
\Sigma\Omega\Sigma=\Sigma
.

Proposition 4

The functor
L:\mathbf{Gauss}\to\mathbf{QuadRel}
is faithful and
\mathbf{GQA}
is conservative over
\overrightarrow{\mathbf{GQA}}
, meaning that
s=t
in
\mathbf{GQA}
implies
s=t
in
\overrightarrow{\mathbf{GQA}}
.

These results provide an elegant and precise connection between the world of Gaussians and of convex optimisation problems. Functoriality of the log-density was laboriously proved in
[
29
]
by explicit means. Here, we obtain the result “for free” from our use of presentations, from which it also easily follows faithfulness and conservativity of
\mathbf{GQA}
over
\overrightarrow{\mathbf{GQA}}
.

Another functor of interest,
S:\mathbf{Gauss}\to\mathbf{AffRel}
can be defined by mapping every generator except
to the same generator in
\mathbf{AffRel}
, and mapping
to
. This functor takes a Gaussian map to the affine relation given by its support; if
f(x)=Ax+\mathcal{N}(b,\Sigma)
, then
S(f):=\{(x,y):y\in Ax+b+\mathrm{im}(\Sigma)\}
.
Again, functoriality of this assignment is an immediate consequence of our presentation results. A similar definition yields a functor
\mathbf{QuadRel}\to\mathbf{AffRel}
, mapping
f:\mathbb{R}^{m+n}\to[0,\infty]
to its effective domain
\text{dom }f=\{(x,y)\mid f(x,y)<\infty\}.

5.2
Ordinary Least-Squares

We now demonstrate how to apply our theory of
\mathbf{GQA}
to the method of ordinary least squares in linear regression.
The aim of linear regression is simple: to find a linear model that best fits a set of observations. In its usual vectorial formulation, all available observations of the regressors form the columns of a single matrix
A
and all observations of the dependent variable form a single vector
y
; then, a linear model with parameters
x
is expressed concisely as the system
Ax=y
. Typically, for consistency, we also assume that the regressors are linearly independent,
i.e.
, that
A
is injective. If
A
is not invertible–as it usually is not–this system does not admit an exact solution. We can nevertheless look for parameters
x
such that
A{x}
best approximates the observed values
y
. Here, ‘best’ is interpreted in such a way that the sum of squared errors,
||y-Ax||^{2}
, is minimised. This function can be translated directly into the following diagram:

The semantics of the last diagram is
{x\choose y}\mapsto\frac{1}{2}\left(||AA^{+}y-Ax||^{2}+||y-AA^{+}y||^{2}\right)
.
Its infimum is clearly reached at
{\hat{x}}=A^{+}y
, as wished: in this case
||AA^{+}y-A{\hat{x}}||^{2}=0
and the remaining term
||y-AA^{+}y||^{2}=||y-A{\hat{x}}||^{2}
indicates the distance between
A{\hat{x}}
and
y
,
i.e.
, how far we are from having successfully inverted
A
.

5.3
Gaussian Probabilistic Programming

In
[
30
,
31
]
the authors study a simple first-order probabilistic programming language for Gaussian probability, which we name
GPL
. The core probabilistic constructs are sampling from a standard-normal distribution
normal
()
and an operator
(\mathrel{\scalebox{0.4}[1]{${=}$}{:}{\scalebox{0.4}[1]{${=}$}}})
for conditioning two random variables to be equal. Terms of
GPL
are, for
\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{R}
,
i\in\{0,1\}
,

\displaystyle s,t::=x\,\,|\,\,s+t\,\,|\,\,\alpha\cdot s\,\,|\,\,\underline{\beta}\,\,|\,\,(s,t)\,\,|\,\,()\,\,|\,\,\mathrm{let}\,{x}\,={s}\,\mathrm{in}\,t\,\,|\,\,s;t\,\,|\,\,\pi_{i}\,s\,\,|\,\,\mathrm{normal}()\,\,|\,\,s\mathrel{\scalebox{0.4}[1]{${=}$}{:}{\scalebox{0.4}[1]{${=}$}}}t

Terms are typed in random variables, see Appendix
J
. In
GPL
we can express an inference problem such as a noisy measurement as follows:

\displaystyle\mathrm{let}\,{x}\,={10\cdot\mathrm{normal}()}\,\mathrm{in}\,\mathrm{let}\,{y}\,={x+5\cdot\mathrm{normal}()}\,\mathrm{in}\,(y\mathrel{\scalebox{0.4}[1]{${=}$}{:}{\scalebox{0.4}[1]{${=}$}}}\underline{40});x

(11)

This expresses the following mathematical problem: If
X\sim\mathcal{N}(0,100)
and
Y|X\sim\mathcal{N}(X,25)
, what is
X|(Y=40)
? The answer turns out to be
\mathcal{N}(32,20)
, which can be found by factorising the joint negative log-density:
f(x,40)\propto\frac{1}{2}\frac{x^{2}}{100}+\frac{1}{2}\frac{(x-40)^{2}}{25}=\frac{1}{2}\frac{(x-32)^{2}}{20}+6.4
.
The constant
c=6.4
at the end corresponds to the
score
of the problem, i.e. the negative logarithm of the
normalisation constant
or
model evidence
. The higher
c
, the less likely was the observation.

It is possible to associate any
GPL
term to a
\mathbf{GQA}
-string diagram. This translation is rigorously definable as a functor, by understanding
GPL
as the internal language of a suitable monoidal category, as discussed in
[
30
,
27
,
13
]
. Given the focus of the present work, we do not pursue this systematically here, and confine ourselves to showing how the constructs of
GPL
map into
\mathbf{GQA}
:

For instance, the program (
11
) translates to the leftmost diagram, and normalises modulo
\mathbf{GQA}
to the posterior distribution and normalisation constant expressed by the rightmost diagram.

\mathrel{\overset{\makebox[0.0pt]{\mbox{\tiny GQA}}}{=}}

Via this translation,
GPL
receives denotational semantics in
\mathbf{QuadRel}
, which is comparable to existing
GPL
semantics in interesting ways: First, the elimination procedure of
Theorem

4.1
mirrors the operational semantics of
[
31
]
by reducing conditioning statements whenever they occur. Second, the normal form argument of
Theorem

4.2
can be also employed to compare two
GPL
terms once understood as
\mathbf{GQA}
diagrams. This may yield a decidability procedure for contextual equivalence, and thus a fully abstract (and completely axiomatised) denotational semantics for
GPL
, which unlike the one in
[
30
]
does not rely on an equivalence relation that is hard to decide. A complete account of this conjecture is outside of the scope of this paper; we leave it for future work.

6
Conclusions

We gave a compositional account of quadratic optimisation via a category of quadratic relations called
\mathbf{QuadRel}
, and provided a complete calculus
\mathbf{GQA}
to reason algebraically about this class of problems. We also showed that a fragment
\overrightarrow{\mathbf{GQA}}
of
\mathbf{GQA}
axiomatises Gaussian probabilistic maps, thus highlighting the relationship between Gaussian probability and convex analysis. We illustrated our approach by discussing functorial tranlations between the Gaussian, quadratic, and affine domain, by modelling the method of ordinary least-squares in linear regression as diagrammatic reasoning, and by giving semantics to probabilistic programming. The last two applications are by no means intended to be the final word on the subject, but rather a starting point for a more systematic treatment. In particular, we plan to give a complete account of full abstraction for Gaussian probabilistic programming, as outlined at the end of
Section

5
. Also, we will further investigate the fragment
\overrightarrow{\mathbf{GQA}}_{\scriptscriptstyle{E}}
and its relationship with extended Gaussian relations. This semantic model is connected with the notion of open stochastic system in Willems’ approach to control theory
[
33
]
, which we should be able to account for similarly to how
\mathbf{GAA}
interprets electrical circuits (
[
4
,
6
]
).

From an algebraic viewpoint, we would like to explore whether the symmetries present in Graphical Affine Algebra extend to Graphical Quadratic Algebra. In particular, we conjecture the ‘colour-swap’ symmetry, mapping eg.
to
and
to
, extends to
\mathbf{GQA}
by mapping
to itself. The semantics of this functor should correspond to convex conjugation (Legendre transformation). Indeed, in convex analysis terminology, every quadratic relation is a so-called convex bifunction (
[
25
]
), which have been studied in categorical terms in
[
29
]
. Independently and at the same time as a preprint
[
32
]
of our work, the authors of
[
8
]
introduced a notion of ‘Gaussian relation’ in the context of quantum computation; their semantics is very different, but their axiomatisation is highly reminiscent of
\mathbf{GQA}
. Their presentation exhibits the colour-swap symmetry discussed earlier, which is interpreted by the Fourier transform. The precise relationship between these approaches remains to be explored.

B
Linear Algebra and Graphical Linear Algebra

We recall some basic facts of linear algebra that will be useful in subsequent proofs. We will use classic matrix notation and string diagrammatic notation interchangeably: this is justified by Proposition
1
, which implies that any equivalence of matrices or subspaces represented by string diagrams are provable in the equational theory of
\mathbf{GAA}
.

A matrix
A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}
is
orthogonal
if
AA^{T}=A^{T}A=I
. A
rotation matrix
is a matrix
A
that is orthogonal and furthermore satisfies
\det(A)=1
. Any orthogonal matrix can be written as a product of a rotation matrix and a reflections. The classic matrix groups are defined as

\displaystyle\mathrm{GL}(n)

\displaystyle=\{A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\text{ invertible }\}

\displaystyle\mathrm{O}(n)

\displaystyle=\{A\in\mathrm{GL}(n)\text{ orthogonal}\}

We recall the following well-known characterisations. Because
\mathbf{GAA}
presents
\mathbf{AffRel}
(Proposition
1
) and
\mathbf{GQA}
is a conservative extension of
\mathbf{GAA}
, we may use them freely while doing diagrammatic reasoning in
\mathbf{GQA}
.

Proposition 5
(Column equivalence)

For two matrices
A,B\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times k}
, the following are equivalent

1.

\mathrm{im}(A)=\mathrm{im}(B)

2.

there exists an invertible matrix
S
with
AS=B
.

Proposition 6
(Orthogonal column equivalence)

For two matrices
A,B\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times k}
, the following are equivalent

1.

AA^{T}=BB^{T}

2.

there exists an orthogonal matrix
R
with
AR=B
.

Two subspaces
S,D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n}
are
complementary
if
S+D=\mathbb{R}^{n}
and
S\cap D=0
. Every vector
x\in R^{n}
decomposes uniquely as
x=x_{S}+x_{D}
with
x_{S}\in S,x_{D}\in D
. We obtain the corresponding projections
P_{S},P_{D}
. A canonical choice of complementary subspace is the orthogonal complement
S=D^{\bot}
.

Proposition 7
(Invariance)

is invariant under
\mathrm{GL}(n)
, i.e. for all invertible matrices
S\in\mathrm{GL}(n)
we have in
\mathbf{GAA}

\underline{S}
=

(GLI)

Proof

The Gaussian elimination algorithm, which we may mimic by equational reasoning in
\mathbf{GAA}
, demonstrates that every invertible matrix can be built up from three kinds of elementary transformations

1.

scaling
x\mapsto\alpha x
, with
\alpha\neq 0

2.

swapping
(x,y)\mapsto(y,x)

3.

the shear mapping
(x,y)\mapsto(x,kx+y)

The generator
is invariant under swapping by the laws of symmetric monoidal categories (Appendix
A
), and under scaling by (SI). It remains to show that it is invariant under the shear mapping:

k
=
k
=
TI

be two matrices satisfying
\mathrm{im}(A)=\mathrm{im}(B)
. Then we can derive in
\mathbf{GAA}

Proposition 9

Proposition 11

The interpretation of
\mathbf{GQA}
in
\mathbf{QuadRel}
is sound.

Proof

\mathbf{AffRel}
embeds in
\mathbf{QuadRel}
via indicator functions of affine relations. Thus all the axioms of
\mathbf{GAA}
are verified. It remains to verify the three axioms involving the quadratic generator, namely (RI), (D) and (Z).

Proof

A
Givens rotation
is a rotation matrix which acts as a rotation along two coordinate axes, and the identity otherwise. From (RI), it follows immediately that
is invariant under Givens rotations. Now we use the fact (proved below) that every orthogonal matrix
R
can be written as a product
R=Q_{1}\cdots Q_{n}\cdot D
where the
Q_{i}
are Givens rotations and
D
is a diagonal matrix with entries
\pm 1
. From this, the proposition follows by repeated application of invariance under Givens rotations and flip invariance (
Proposition

12
).

It remains to prove the claimed decomposition of
R
, which we establish as follows: The usual algorithm for QR-decomposition gives
R=QU
, where
Q
is a product of Givens rotations and
U
is upper triangular. Then
U=Q^{T}R
is orthogonal (normal) in addition to being upper triangular, hence must be diagonal, with entries
\pm 1
. All of these linear algebraic transformations can be performed diagrammatically in
\overrightarrow{\mathbf{GQA}}
, by Proposition
1
.

E
Quadratic Relations

We give the proofs missing in
Section

4.1
.
We will use the following characterisation.

Proposition 16

The following are equivalent for a function
f:\mathbb{R}^{n}\to[-\infty,\infty]

1.

f
is a nonnegative partial quadratic function

2.

f
can be written in the form
f(x)=h(A(x-a))+c

where
A
is an invertible matrix,
c\geq 0
and
h
an elementary convex partial quadratic function

3.

f
can be written as
f(x)=\inf\left\{{||y||^{2}:(x,y)\in M}\right\}

where
M\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n}\times\mathbb{R}^{m}
is an affine subspace.

Let us first describe the meaning of these statements.
Item

2
is an analogue of Sylvester’s law of inertia for partial quadratic functions; in fact, it suffices to allow the values
\lambda_{i}\in\{0,1,\infty\}
on the diagonal. Item 3 shows that nonnegative partial convex functions are precisely the class of functions that arise in constrained least squares optimisation
[
9
]
, which justifies our choice of using them as the morphisms of the semantic domain
\mathbf{QuadRel}
.

Proof
(Proof of
Proposition

16
)

(1)\Rightarrow(2)
using an affine coordinate change, we can assume that the domain of
f
is the subspace
M=\mathbb{R}^{m}\times\{0\}
. The restricted function
\tilde{f}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{m})=f(x_{1},\ldots,x_{m},0,\ldots,0)
is a total nonnegative quadratic function so we can apply the characterisation
Proposition

16
to
\tilde{f}
to obtain the desired form

f(x)=h(A((x_{1},\ldots,x_{m})-a))+\infty\cdot x_{m+1}+\ldots+\infty\cdot x_{n}+c

(2)\Rightarrow(3)
Under the affine coordinate change
\mathbf{y}=A(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{a})
, it suffices to consider
f(\mathbf{y})=h(\mathbf{y})+c
where
h
is an elementary quadratic function of the form
h(\mathbf{y_{1}},\mathbf{y_{2}},\mathbf{y_{3}})=||\mathbf{y_{1}}||^{2}+\{\!|\,{\mathbf{y_{3}}=0}\,|\!\}
. In this case, we can define the affine relation

M=\{((\mathbf{y_{1}},\mathbf{y_{2}},\mathbf{y_{3}}),(\mathbf{y_{1}},\sqrt{c}))\,\,|\,\,\mathbf{y_{3}}=0\}

and have
f(x)=\inf\left\{{||z||^{2}:(x,z)\in M}\right\}
.

(3)\Rightarrow(1)
If
M\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n}\times\mathbb{R}^{m}
is an affine relation, then there exists a vector subspace
D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n}
and an affine map
g:\mathbb{R}^{n}\to D^{\bot}
such that

M_{x}=\begin{cases}g(x)+D,&x\in\pi_{X}M\\
\emptyset,&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}

where
M_{X}=\{y:(x,y)\in M\}
. Thus we have

\inf\left\{{||y||^{2}:y\in M_{x}}\right\}=||g(x)||^{2}+\{\!|\,{x\in\pi_{X}M}\,|\!\}

which is evidently a nonnegative partial quadratic function.

We are now ready for the proof of
Proposition

2
.

Proof
(Proof of
Proposition

2
)

Let
g:\mathbb{R}^{m}\to[-\infty,\infty]
be a nonnegative partial quadratic function and
M\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{m}\times\mathbb{R}^{n}
an affine relation. Using the representation of
Proposition

16
and an affine coordinate change, it suffices to consider the case where
g
is an elementary function, i.e. a constrained minimization problem of the form

f(x)=\inf\left\{{||\mathbf{y_{1}}||^{2}+\{\!|\,{\mathbf{y_{3}}=0}\,|\!\}:(x,(\mathbf{y_{1}},\mathbf{y_{2}},\mathbf{y_{3}}))\in M}\right\}

We define the affine relation
M^{\prime}=\{(x,\mathbf{y_{1}}):(x,(\mathbf{y_{1}},\mathbf{y_{2}},0))\in M\}
and conclude that
f(x)=\inf\left\{{||y||^{2}:(x,y)\in M^{\prime}}\right\}
which is a partial quadratic function by
Proposition

16
.

F
Completeness for Extended Gaussian Processes

An
extended Gaussian distribution
is a Gaussian distribution on a quotient space
\mathbb{R}^{n}/D
; the vector subspace
D
is called a
nondeterministic fibre
. This concept intends to model the idea of a distribution carrying both a probabilistic and a nondeterministic component. We can write it in additive notation
\mathcal{N}(\mu,\Sigma)+D
, where we think of the subspace
D
as an idealised uniform distribution. Extended Gaussians support the same basic transformations as ordinary Gaussians, such as pushforwards and conditioning
[
28
]
. A related notion appears in Willems’ approach to control theory, under the name of open stochastic system
[
33
]
. A major reason of interest for extended Gaussians is that they give semantics to Gaussian probabilistic programming extended with a construct
\mathsf{uniform}()
to sample from a uniform prior
[
28
,
29
]
.

Similarly to Gaussian maps (
Section

3
), one may define a notion of extended Gaussian map, informally written as
f(x)=Ax+\mathcal{N}(\mu,\Sigma)+D
, where
Ax+\mathcal{N}(\mu,\Sigma)
is a Gaussian map and
D
is the nondeterministic component. A prop
\mathbf{GaussEx}
of these maps is defined
[
28
]
.

We first recall the complete definition of the prop
\mathbf{GaussEx}
of extended Gaussian maps.

Definition 7
(
[
28
]
)

The prop
\mathbf{GaussEx}
has morphisms
m\to n
pairs
(m\xrightarrow{A}k\xleftarrow{P}n,\varphi)
, where
m\xrightarrow{A}k\xleftarrow{P}n
is a cospan in
\mathbf{Vect}
,
P
is surjective, and
\varphi
is a morphism of type
0\to k
in
\mathbf{Gauss}
, i.e. a Gaussian distribution
\mathcal{N}(\mu,\Sigma)
on
\mathbb{R}^{k}
. In additive notation, we may represent such a morphism as
f(x)=Ax+\mathcal{N}(\mu^{\prime},\Sigma^{\prime})+D
, where the kernel subspace
D:=\ker(P)
is the nondeterministic fibre, and
\mu^{\prime}:=Q\mu
,
\Sigma^{\prime}:=Q\Sigma Q^{T}
for some right-inverse
Q
of
P
. Note
f(x)
selects one element
z\in D
of the fibre, which we can interpret as the non-deterministic choice of
f
.

The monoidal product of
(m\xrightarrow{A}k\xleftarrow{P}n,\varphi)
and
(m^{\prime}\xrightarrow{A^{\prime}}k^{\prime}\xleftarrow{P^{\prime}}n^{\prime},\varphi^{\prime})
is defined as
(m+m^{\prime}\xrightarrow{A\oplus A^{\prime}}k+k^{\prime}\xleftarrow{P\oplus P^{\prime}}n+n^{\prime},\varphi\oplus\varphi^{\prime})
, using the monoidal product in
\mathbf{Vect}
on the cospan legs and the one in
\mathbf{Gauss}
on the distributions. The sequential composition of
(m_{1}\xrightarrow{A_{1}}k_{1}\xleftarrow{P_{1}}n,\varphi_{1})
and
(n\xrightarrow{A_{2}}k_{2}\xleftarrow{P_{2}}n_{2},\varphi_{2})
is defined as
(m_{1}\xrightarrow{A_{1};L}k\xleftarrow{P_{2};R}n_{2},\varphi)
, where
k_{1}\xrightarrow{L}k\xleftarrow{R}k_{2}
is the pushout of
k_{1}\xleftarrow{P_{1}}n\xrightarrow{A_{1}}k_{2}
in
\mathbf{Vect}
,
in
\mathbf{Vect}
and
\varphi
is the convolution in
\mathbf{Gauss}
of distributions
\varphi_{1};L\colon 0\to k
and
\varphi_{2};R\colon 0\to k
.
4
4

4

As usual, for composition by pushout to be well-defined, strictly speaking morphisms of this category are equivalence classes of isomorphic cospans.

One may phrase
\mathbf{GaussEx}
more abstractly as a category of ‘decorated’ cospans
[
14
]
, see
[
28
]
for details. Also,
\mathbf{GaussEx}
is a Markov category
[
15
]
. Note there is an embedding
\mathbf{Gauss}\to\mathbf{GaussEx}
where
(A,b,\Sigma)
is sent to the cospan
(m\xrightarrow{A}n\xleftarrow{Id}n,\mathcal{N}(b,\Sigma))
whose right leg is the identity, i.e. the nondeterministic fibre vanishes. Also there is an embedding
\mathbf{GaussEx}\to\mathbf{QuadRel}
mapping the cospan
(m\xrightarrow{A}k\xleftarrow{P}n,\mathcal{N}(b,\Sigma))
to the negative log-likelihood function

\begin{split}f(x,y)=\langle Py-Ax-b,\Sigma^{+}(Py-Ax-b)\rangle+\\
\{\!|\,{Py-Ax-b\in\mathrm{im}(\Sigma)}\,|\!\}.\end{split}

with
\Sigma^{+}
the Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse of
\Sigma
. This embedding is discussed in
[
29
]
. Proving functoriality is highly non-trivial, but it becomes a simple corrollary when paired with our presentation results, see
Section

5.1
.

M:m\to n
be any string diagram in
\overrightarrow{\mathbf{GQA}}_{\scriptscriptstyle{E}}

M
can be brought into the form

\underline{D}

Proof
(Proof of
Theorem

0..1
)

The proof consists in verifying definability, soundness, and completeness under the prop morphism
\left\langle\!\left\langle{\cdot}\right\rangle\!\right\rangle
.
First we show definability. Let
f=(m\xrightarrow{A}k\xleftarrow{P}n,\mathcal{N}(\mu,\Sigma))
be a morphism of
\mathbf{GaussEx}
, informally representing the map
f(x)=Ax+\mathcal{N}(\mu,\Sigma)+D
where
D=\ker(P)
. Then
f
is definable by the term

\underline{D}
\underline{\mathcal{N}(\mu,\Sigma)}
\underline{A}

(12)

For completeness, we note that the form (
12
) is not quite a normal for
\mathbf{GaussEx}
semantics, but it becomes one if we insist on the further conditions that

\mu\in D^{\bot},\mathrm{im}(A)\subseteq D^{\bot},\mathrm{im}(\Sigma)\subseteq D^{\bot}

where
D^{\bot}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n}
is the orthogonal complement of
D
.
As detailed in
Proposition

17
, we can transform every string diagram of
\overrightarrow{\mathbf{GQA}}_{\scriptscriptstyle{E}}
into that specific shape. The values of
D,A,\mu,\Sigma
are then uniquely determined from the interpretation
\left\langle\!\left\langle{\cdot}\right\rangle\!\right\rangle
in
\mathbf{GaussEx}
.

) instead simplifies as

\underline{R}
\underline{c}
=
N
\underline{c}
N
\underline{R}
\mathrel{\overset{\makebox[0.0pt]{\mbox{\tiny RI}}}{=}}
N
\underline{c}
M^{\prime}

where the scalar is either
0
or
\infty
depending on whether
c=0
.

Then the scalars are normalised separately according to the procedure of Appendix
G
.

We now give further lemmas needed for the proof of completeness of
\mathbf{GQA}
.

First, recall that a
generalised inverse
of a matrix
A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times m}
is a matrix
G\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}
such that
AGA=A
; that is, for all
y\in\mathrm{im}(A)
we have that
Gy
is a preimage of
y
. Every matrix has a generalised inverse, but it is generally not unique as there are two degrees of freedom: What shall
G
do outside of the image
\mathrm{im}(A)
, and which preimage of
y
should it pick? The
Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse

A^{+}
is a particularly well-known generalized inverse which answers both questions by projecting orthogonally.

The Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse gives an explicit solution to least-squares problem:

\inf\{||x||^{2}:Ax=y\}

is attained at
x=A^{+}y
when
y\in\mathrm{im}(A)
.

where
A^{+}
is the Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse of
A
. This expression is furthermore equal to

\frac{1}{2}\langle y,\Omega y\rangle+\{\!|\,{y\in\mathrm{im}(A)}\,|\!\}

where
\Omega
is any generalized inverse of
AA^{T}
.

Proof

The denotation corresponds to the quadratic problem

\inf_{{x}}\left\{{\frac{1}{2}||x||^{2}+\{\!|\,{y=Ax}\,|\!\}}\right\}=\inf\left\{{\frac{1}{2}||x||^{2}:y=Ax}\right\}

which is solved using the Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse. We have

\langle A^{+}y,A^{+}y\rangle=\langle y,(A^{+})^{T}A^{+}y\rangle=\langle y,\Omega y\rangle

As a Corollary of
Proposition

24
and
Proposition

21
, we can compute the following semantics.

Proposition 25

In
\mathbf{QuadRel}
, we have

\left\llbracket{\underline{\mathcal{N}(\mu,\Sigma)}}\right\rrbracket(x)=\frac{1}{2}\langle(x-\mu),\Omega(x-\mu)\rangle+\{\!|\,{(x-\mu)\in\mathrm{im}(\Sigma)}\,|\!\}

where
\Omega
is any generalized inverse of
\Sigma
.

(14)

Then
D_{1}=D_{2}
,
\mu_{1}=\mu_{2}
and
\Sigma_{1}=\Sigma_{2}
.

Proof

Let
f:\mathbb{R}^{n}\to[0,\infty]
be the quadratic relation denoted by (
14
). Then we can read off the space
D_{1}=D_{2}
as the largest subspace along which
f
is constant (
Proposition

22
). Restricting
f
along the complement
D^{\bot}
, we obtain the denotation of the Gaussian distribution in
Proposition

25
, from which
\mu
and
\Sigma
can be determined.

Proof
(Proof of

)

Faithfulness is clear as every Gaussian map can be reconstructed from its log-density. For conservativity, if two

-terms

are provably equal in
\mathbf{GQA}
, then

is provable in

by completeness.

I
More Details on Ordinary Least Squares in
\mathbf{GQA}

In this appendix we expand Section
5.2
, showing how to apply our theory of
\mathbf{GQA}
to the method of ordinary least squares in linear regression. The aim of linear regression is simple: to find a linear model that best fits a set of observations. In its usual vectorial formulation, all available observations of the regressors form the columns of a single matrix
A
and all observations of the dependent variable form a single vector
y
; then, a linear model with parameters
x
is expressed concisely as the system
Ax=y
. Typically, for consistency, we also assume that the regressors are linearly independent,
i.e.
, that
A
is injective. If
A
is not invertible–as it usually isn’t–this system does not admit an exact solution. We can nevertheless look for parameters
x
such that
A{x}
best approximates the observed values
y
. Here, ‘best’ is interpreted in such a way that the sum of squared errors,
||y-Ax||^{2}
, is minimised. This function can be translated directly into the following diagram:

The formula for the optimal
\hat{x}
is well-known to be the familiar ordinary least squares (OLS) estimator
\hat{x}=(A^{T}A)^{-1}A^{T}y=A^{+}y
. Our aim here is to re-derive this expression starting from the diagram above, using the axioms of
\mathbf{GQA}
.
We then need a lemma which, in semantic terms, states that
||Ax+y||^{2}=||Ax||^{2}+||y||^{2}
when
A^{T}y=0
,
i.e.
, when
y
is in the kernel of the transpose of
A
,
i.e.
, is orthogonal to the image of
A
. It is easy to see why this holds:
||Ax+y||^{2}=||Ax||^{2}+2\langle Ax,y\rangle+||y||^{2}
and since
A^{T}y=0
, we have
\langle Ax,y\rangle=\langle x,A^{T}y\rangle=0
. We now derive it diagrammatically. Note that this is the only part of our derivation of the OLS estimator which uses the
quadratic
fragment of GQA; the rest will be plain GAA.

Proof

We will need a few useful facts from (graphical) linear algebra. First, recall that a matrix
A
can be written
UDV^{T}
, where
U,V
are orthogonal matrices and
D
is diagonal—this is known as the
singular value decomposition
(SVD) of
A
. Diagrammatically, this translates to the two equalities on the first line below (and the two on the second line for the transpose of
A
):

\displaystyle\hbox to28.14pt{\vbox to11.76pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 14.96916pt\lower-5.42505pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin=1} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke=#000000} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill=#000000} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width=0.4pt} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin=1} \hbox to0.0pt{

\lxSVG@closescope {

{{}}{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\hbox{\hbox{{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin=1} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill=#FFFFFF} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke=#000000} {{}{}{{

where once again, the equality (
*
) uses the fact that
V
is orthogonal and
C
diagonal and thus their kernel is trivial.

We also record the following lemma, which is just linear algebra, so we appeal to completeness of
\mathbf{GQA}
for the proof. Intuitively, it translates the fact that
I-AA^{+}
is the projection onto the orthogonal space to the range of
A
,
i.e.
onto the the kernel of
A^{T}
. (Note also that
AA^{+}
is the projection onto the range of
A
.)

The semantics of the last diagram is the quadratic function

{x\choose y}\mapsto\frac{1}{2}\left(||AA^{+}y-Ax||^{2}+||y-AA^{+}y||^{2}\right).

Its infimum is clearly reached at
{\hat{x}}=A^{+}y
as we wanted: in this case
||AA^{+}y-A{\hat{x}}||^{2}=0
and the remaining term
||y-AA^{+}y||^{2}=||y-A{\hat{x}}||^{2}
indicates the distance between
A{\hat{x}}
and
y
,
i.e.
, how far we are from having successfully inverted
A
.

J
Typing Judgements for
GPL

Types
\tau
are generated from a basic type
\mathrm{R}
denoting
real
or
random variable
, pair types and unit type
I
. That is,
\tau::=\mathrm{R}\,\,|\,\,\mathrm{I}\,\,|\,\,\tau\ast\tau
. Typing judgements are as follows.

\Gamma,x:\tau,\Gamma^{\prime}\vdash x:\tau\qquad\Gamma\vdash():\mathrm{I}\qquad\Gamma\vdash(s,t):\sigma\ast\tau\Gamma\vdash s:\sigma\quad\Gamma\vdash t:\tau

\Gamma\vdash s+t:\mathrm{R}\Gamma\vdash s:\mathrm{R}\quad\Gamma\vdash t:\mathrm{R}\qquad\Gamma\vdash\alpha\cdot t:\mathrm{R}\Gamma\vdash t:\mathrm{R}\qquad\Gamma\vdash\underline{\beta}:\mathrm{R}

\Gamma\vdash\mathrm{normal}():\mathrm{R}\qquad\Gamma\vdash(s\mathrel{\scalebox{0.4}[1]{${=}$}{:}{\scalebox{0.4}[1]{${=}$}}}t):\mathrm{I}\Gamma\vdash s:\mathrm{R}\quad\Gamma\vdash t:\mathrm{R}

\Gamma\vdash s;t:\tau\Gamma\vdash s:I\quad\Gamma\vdash t:\tau

\Gamma\vdash\mathrm{let}\,{x}\,={s}\,\mathrm{in}\,t:\tau\Gamma\vdash s:\sigma\quad\Gamma,x:\sigma\vdash t:\tau\qquad\Gamma\vdash\pi_{i}\,e:\tau_{i}\Gamma\vdash e:\tau_{1}\ast\tau_{2}
